title: Job 31:1–12
context: Chapter 31 closes the long speech Job began in chapter 29: having recalled his former honor (chapter 29) and his present humiliation (chapter 30), he now takes an oath of clearance, a chain of conditional self-curses that pair an “if I have” clause with a “then let” penalty In 31:1–12 he disowns lustful looking, falsehood, greed, and adultery. The oath is Job’s final protest of integrity. It answers charges the friends have pressed (compare Eliphaz in 22:5–9), but the friends have not refuted it, and the book’s later verdict (42:7) is left to do its own work. The lines on desire and adultery are about inward and outward faithfulness; the notes treat them soberly and without elaboration. Both traditions read Job’s claim to integrity as a claim to sincere, wholehearted devotion, in line with the narrator’s description of him in 1:1, not as a claim to sinless perfection.

verses.text: “I made a covenant with my eyes; how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?
verses.arminianNotes: Job says he made a covenant with his eyes not to look lustfully at a young woman. Arminian readers note that Job begins with the inward life, a deliberate commitment of the will that he renewed and kept by choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the verse an awareness that faithfulness starts with the heart and the gaze, compare Matthew 5:28 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the line soberly as Job’s claim to inward purity, not mere outward restraint.

verses.text: For what is the portion from God above, and the heritage from the Almighty on high?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks what portion and heritage come from God above. Arminian readers see Job reasoning about the moral order: he restrained himself because he believed the Almighty assigns each person a real outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job’s question assumes God as the one who allots every person’s lot from on high. Both traditions read the verse as Job’s motive for self-restraint: reverent awareness of the God who judges.

verses.text: Is it not calamity to the unrighteous, and disaster to the workers of iniquity?
verses.arminianNotes: Job says calamity and disaster belong to the unrighteous and the workers of iniquity. Arminian readers note the irony that this was the friends’ own principle, and Job’s suffering seems to contradict it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Job still holds to divine justice even while his experience strains it. Shared ground: both traditions see the tension the book is exploring, without letting the friends’ rigid formula settle it.

verses.text: Doesn’t he see my ways, and count all my steps?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether God does not see his ways and count his steps. Arminian readers see Job appealing to God’s full knowledge as a witness that he has walked honestly, and as the reason he kept watch on himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an affirmation that no step escapes God’s notice, a truth Job finds both sobering and, here, reassuring. Both traditions read the line as confidence that God knows the truth of Job’s life.

verses.text: “If I have walked with falsehood, and my foot has hurried to deceit
verses.arminianNotes: Job begins his formal oath, disowning falsehood and a foot that hurried to deceit. Arminian readers note that the oath form places Job’s integrity under judgment, inviting scrutiny rather than avoiding it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job’s denial concerns a settled way of life, not the absence of every failing. Shared ground: both traditions read the opening oath as Job staking his whole conduct on the truth of his words.

verses.text: (let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know my integrity);
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks to be weighed in an even balance so that God may know his integrity. Arminian readers see Job trusting that a fair weighing would vindicate the real faithfulness he has practiced.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scales as an image of exact justice and note that Job wants a hearing, not leniency. Both traditions read the parenthesis as Job’s appeal for honest judgment, made in the open before God.

verses.text: if my step has turned out of the way, if my heart walked after my eyes, if any defilement has stuck to my hands,
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns turning aside from the way, letting his heart follow his eyes, or having defilement stick to his hands. Arminian readers see the links between seeing, desiring, and doing, which Job claims he has resisted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the movement from eyes to heart to hands, tracing how sin moves from desire to deed. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s claim that his inner life and outward acts have stayed clean.

verses.text: then let me sow, and let another eat. Yes, let the produce of my field be rooted out.
verses.arminianNotes: Job calls for a fitting penalty if he is guilty: let him sow and another eat, and his produce be rooted out. Arminian readers note the seriousness of the self-curse, which shows how firmly Job believes his own claim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the penalty as matching the offense, loss of the fruit of one’s labor for a life of grasping. Both traditions read the self-curse as part of the legal form of the oath, not as a casual turn of speech.

verses.text: “If my heart has been enticed to a woman, and I have laid wait at my neighbor’s door,
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns being enticed toward a woman and lying in wait at his neighbor’s door. Arminian readers note that he addresses both the inward pull and the outward scheming, and claims to have refused both.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as covering desire and premeditated betrayal of a neighbor. Shared ground: both traditions read the line soberly as a denial of adultery, a wrong against God, the neighbor, and the neighbor’s household.

verses.text: then let my wife grind for another, and let others sleep with her.
verses.arminianNotes: Job states a self-curse touching his own wife if he were guilty of adultery. Arminian readers note that the imagery reflects the ancient world’s sense of fitting retribution and should not be read as approving harm to the wife.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the line as the language of an oath in Job’s culture, stressing the gravity of the offense rather than prescribing a penalty. Both traditions handle the verse soberly and do not dwell on its imagery.

verses.text: For that would be a heinous crime. Yes, it would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges,
verses.arminianNotes: Job calls adultery a heinous crime, an iniquity to be punished by the judges. Arminian readers note that Job treats the sin as a public wrong as well as a private one, harming the community’s trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as recognizing that marriage is guarded by both divine and human law. Shared ground: both traditions read Job’s words as a sober judgment on the seriousness of breaking faith in marriage.

verses.text: for it is a fire that consumes to destruction, and would root out all my increase.
verses.arminianNotes: Job compares adultery to a fire that consumes to destruction, rooting out all his increase. Arminian readers see a warning that such sin spreads its damage far beyond the moment, ruining a whole life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image echoes the wisdom tradition’s warnings about adultery’s destructive results. Both traditions read the verse as Job explaining why he refused the path: it destroys what it touches.
